cd35cf8e-d1f1-4752-8183-b4b90095f456.one_liner: Mostly an Asian-equities/bank-stock pitch on undervalued North Asian FX, but touches BOJ/BOK tightening, rising long-end UST yields, Fed curve-control chatter ahead of Jackson Hole, and PBOC's offshore CNY settlement expansion in Hong Kong.
cd35cf8e-d1f1-4752-8183-b4b90095f456.recap: Mizuho equity strategist Sean Darby argues North Asian currencies (yen, won, Taiwan dollar, yuan) are trading 40-56% undervalued versus the dollar on purchasing-power-parity grounds (illustrated via the Big Mac index, dubbed 'Burger Heaven'), despite these economies holding the world's largest FX reserves and running large trade/current-account surpluses. He attributes the undervaluation partly to structural capital outflows (Korean retail and Taiwanese life-insurer buying of US assets) chasing wider US rate differentials. That is now reversing: the Bank of Korea hiked 25bp, Bank of Japan has moved from negative to 1% and may hike twice more into 2027, and Taiwan's central bank, on hold since 2024 despite strong data, faces mounting pressure to follow. Retail sales, nominal GDP (up to 16% YoY) and shipbuilding orders are surging on AI-driven export booms, spilling into domestic demand and inflation. Darby's trade idea is North Asian bank stocks, which he says are under-owned versus AI/tech names but stand to benefit from steepening yield curves and rising deposit-lending spreads, citing Japanese bank ROEs rising from ~5% pre-COVID to over 10% now. Separately, he discusses China's currency strength (large trade surplus, PBOC gold buying, and a new PBOC electronic settlement scheme allowing offshore CNY settlement in Hong Kong) as part of a de-dollarization push. He also flags a sticky-inflation, rising-yield backdrop in the US (30-year UST above 5.2%) and speculates that ahead of Jackson Hole, Fed's Warsh will focus on the front end (up to 90 days) while Besant manages the long end, effectively attempting to cap yields.

eee35f63-91d3-4b60-85e5-aabc8ccd7e80.one_liner: A rates-macro commentary arguing Fed hawkishness (Warsh) is fighting a fragile labor market and an un-inverting curve, not real inflation risk -- directly bears on front-end rates positioning.
eee35f63-91d3-4b60-85e5-aabc8ccd7e80.recap: The speaker ties together three recent events: Kevin Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole remarks favoring rate hikes to fight above-target CPI/PCE inflation, Treasury Secretary Besant's public pushback that the economy is facing an oil-driven supply shock that shouldn't warrant hiking absent second-order effects, and Tuesday's JOLTS report. The core argument is that the Fed fixates on the headline unemployment rate and inflation mandate while ignoring the JOLTS hiring rate, which fell back to roughly 5 million (near cycle lows, comparable to early-2010s levels) and stayed below the ~2% threshold that historically triggers labor-force dropouts. Because discouraged workers exit the labor force and stop counting as unemployed, the official unemployment rate understates real labor-market weakness, and negative net turnover for a third straight month raises the odds of a negative August payroll print. The speaker contrasts this with TIPS breakevens, which remain low despite rising oil prices, arguing the market is pricing demand destruction rather than inflation -- reinforced by Eurozone August CPI hitting a three-year high on energy alone while core CPI unexpectedly decelerated to 2.4%. On rates, the speaker argues the 30-year yield is barely changed since 2023 and spreads (30yr-3mo, 10yr-30yr) have compressed sharply despite far higher debt issuance, meaning there is no Treasury-rejection or term-premium story; instead this is ordinary curve un-inversion being resisted by the Fed's front-end stickiness, which risks re-inverting the curve if the Fed keeps hiking rhetoric.
terms: JOLTS -- Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, a BLS release covering hires, quits, and turnover
PCE deflator -- Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge
TIPS breakevens -- the market-implied inflation rate derived from the yield spread between nominal Treasuries and Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities
HICP -- Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices, the Eurozone's standardized CPI measure
